the women experienced the HIV infection as a life-changing event that affected them in many ways, and that the sociocultural context in which they lived had a major impact on their responses to HIV infection.

the Cambodian women infected with HIV through their husbands had a delayed diagnosis of HIV, had to deal not only with the physical and mental consequences of the disease but also with the social consequences of being HIV-positive and, as a result, had to deal both with the fear of rejection and with the fear of being discriminated against by their families, communities and society.
women who are HIV positive as a result of transmission by their spouse have to deal with a number of complex emotions, including fear, shame, sadness and guilt.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the lived experiences of Cambodian female spouses who were infected with HIV by a husband who was also HIV positive, and how they dealt with the diagnosis.
the lived experiences of Cambodian HIV-positive women as they discovered, disclosed and dealt with the diagnosis.

the experiences of women who are infected with HIV by spouses, and the ways in which they navigate the tasks of discovering the HIV status, dealing with the diagnosis, and going public about their HIV status.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
women’s lived experiences of HIV infection are influenced by the sociocultural and political context within which they live.
women who are infected with HIV by a husband have to deal with the consequences of the diagnosis within their own social network and in their own cultural context.

, for these Cambodian women, becoming HIV-positive meant that they had to deal with a number of challenges, including finding themselves to be infected with a stigmatized illness, accepting the unwelcomed guest, and dealing with the fear that others would find out about the infection and discriminate against them.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
women infected by their husbands have to deal with the diagnosis and the fear of discrimination, while at the same time having to cope with a sociocultural context that is often unfavourable to them.
women who were infected with HIV by spouses in Cambodia had to face many challenges and barriers in the process of becoming a person with HIV.
the Cambodian socioculture is not only an obstacle to the prevention of HIV transmission from husbands to wives but also a significant barrier to the disclosure of HIV status.
The main takeaway from our work is that

women’s experiences of living with HIV in Cambodia are unique, and that the women in our study had a difficult time coping with the diagnosis, disclosing their HIV status, and dealing with the discrimination and stigma associated with HIV infection.
HIV prevention and care programmes must be culturally sensitive to the needs of women in Cambodia, particularly in the area of HIV disclosure and the stigma associated with HIV infection.
HIV prevention and care interventions for women need to be culturally appropriate and sensitive to the sociocultural and gendered roles and responsibilities in the Cambodian context.
